meta.title: Navajo A1 Beginner
meta.subtitle: 500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Navajo → English (see the Navajo, recall the meaning) and English → Navajo (see an English meaning, recall the Navajo). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 500 words for a complete beginner, aligned to A1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand and use familiar everyday expressions and very basic phrases aimed at the satisfaction of needs of a concrete type' — a learner here is able to introduce themselves and others, to ask and answer questions about personal details such as where they live, people they know and things they have, and to interact in a simple way provided the other person talks slowly and clearly and is prepared to help. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no exam board publishes a graded word list for Navajo (Diné bizaad), so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 294 of the 500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — greetings and politeness, introducing yourself, family and kinship, numbers, the times of day and the seasons, food and drink, animals, the home and the town, the body and feeling ill, the weather and the land, colours, the everyday verbs, and the pronouns, question words, postpositions and particles every sentence is built out of — and the other 206 are the commonest remaining words found in BOTH of two small corpora: the Navajo Wikipedia and the example sentences of English Wiktionary's Navajo entries. Each word is counted by the WHOLE word (a noun's possessed forms and a verb's persons added together), and a word must be in both, since the Wikipedia is mostly short articles about animals and plants. The cards are dealt by that count, so the words you meet most often come first. Every headword is printed in the standard Navajo spelling, which writes what English spelling has no letter for: a high tone with an acute accent (á), a nasal vowel with a hook (ą), a long vowel doubled (aa), the glottal stop as ʼ, and ł for the sound of Welsh ll. 288 of the 500 words also show their pronunciation in the International Phonetic Alphabet, where English Wiktionary gives it. A verb is given as Navajo dictionaries cite it, in the third person ('he/she is eating it'), with its 'I' and 'you' forms where the source has them; a noun for a relative or a part of the body is always somebody's in Navajo, and the card prints it as 'my …' and 'his/her …' (shimá, bimá 'mother'). Real example sentences come with 404 of the 500 words, three apiece for 216 of them, with the word picked out in colour; they are English Wiktionary's own usage examples and, for a few, Tatoeba's. There is no read-aloud button: no device carries a Navajo voice, and one without it reads the word in English. The Navajo Alphabet deck, the first in this collection, teaches the letters and sounds. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, forms, pronunciation and most example sentences: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: the Navajo Wikipedia (dump of 2026-11-01, CC BY-SA 4.0) and Wiktionary's examples. A few sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
